passage:
Friday. Second retro since I set the same-day review rule. Sticky notes on the glass wall again: green for what worked, pink for what didn't. Two weeks ago there were nine pink notes, and almost all of them said the same thing: code reviews sitting for days. Sarita counted, and the average wait had been three days. I'd been one of the slow reviewers too. So the rule was simple: every review gets a first reply the same day, even if it's only "I'll look properly tomorrow morning." Today there are three pink notes. Reviews now wait less than a day, and the team closed more tickets this fortnight than in any before it. I felt a bit proud, and a bit relieved.

Aadhya

qa.q: How many pink notes were on the wall at this retro?
qa.a: There were three pink notes at this retro.

qa.q: How does Aadhya feel about how the review rule has worked?
qa.a: Aadhya feels a little proud and relieved that the rule has helped the team.

qa.q: What else could the team try to keep improving, and why?
qa.a: The team could rotate a review buddy each week, because sharing the job stops reviews from piling up on one or two people.

qa.q: How might Sarita see the changes?
qa.a: Sarita, who counted the waiting time, probably feels satisfied to see that count lead to a visible improvement.

grounding: Illustrates a fortnightly retrospective where a lead notices slow code reviews, sets a same-day review rule and sees the team's pace improve.

In the small software office above a bank in Hubli, Kalyani led her first team of five. Every second Friday she ran a retrospective in the tiny meeting room, with a whiteboard split into two halves: "worked" and "didn't".
In March, the "didn't" side filled with the same complaint. "Waiting for code review." "My fix sat for three days." "I forgot what I'd changed by the time someone looked."
Kalyani counted the notes aloud. "Five out of six. So this is the real problem." She thought for a moment. "What if every review is done the same day it's requested? Even a first look."
Raghav, the senior developer, frowned. "Some days that's a lot."
"Then we'll see how it feels and change it at the next retro."
Two weeks later, the "didn't" side had nothing about reviews. The sprint board showed eight more tasks finished than before. Raghav admitted, "It's less work than I thought."

qa.q: How many notes complained about code review?
qa.a: Five out of six notes did.

qa.q: How did Raghav feel about the same-day rule at first?
qa.a: Raghav was doubtful and worried it would be too much work on some days.

qa.q: What else could Kalyani do if reviews start slipping again?
qa.a: She could raise it at the next retro and adjust the rule with the team, since the retro itself is where the plan changes.

qa.q: How does the rule look to Raghav two weeks later?
qa.a: Raghav admits it is less work than he feared, seeing the team finish eight more tasks.

grounding: Shows a lead running a retrospective every second Friday, noticing reviews wait for days, setting a same-day review rule and improving pace.
